title.zh: 软糖熊软体物理场景

summary.en: An interactive single-file HTML/three.js scene of translucent, jelly-like gummy bears with soft-body physics was built with Claude Opus 5.5, compared against a stiffer Gemini 4 Argon version using the same prompt.

prompt.text:
Build "Gummy Bears" - a single self-contained HTML file (three.js from a CDN is the only dependency): a handful of translucent gummy bears on a white table that you can grab, stretch, squash, throw and pour.

The bears
- Classic gummy bear silhouette: round head with two ears, short snout, plump body, stubby arms and legs, tiny molded eyes and nose
- Every part melts smoothly into the next - build the body as an implicit surface (metaballs / marching cubes), not separate spheres
- Material: real gummy candy. Translucent with transmission and refraction, colored light absorption that gets deeper in thick parts, glossy clearcoat with sharp highlights
- Colors: cherry red, orange, lemon yellow, apple green, clear pineapple
- Soft colored shadow under each bear, tinted by the bear's own color

Physics (this is the whole point - it must feel like jelly, not plastic)
- Each bear is a soft body: mass points for head, ears, snout, body, belly, hands and feet, held together by volume-preserving shape matching
- Limbs and neck are rendered as stretchy strands between points, getting thinner as they stretch
- Grab any part and pull: it stretches like rubber, the rest of the bear leans after it, on release it snaps back with a damped wobble
- Pull the head up: the neck stretches, the body follows, on release the bear squashes and hops
- Press down on the head: the bear pancakes, bulges sideways, then launches itself back up
- Throw a bear: it flies, squashes on landing, bounces and pushes other bears out of the way
- Bears collide with each other and never pass through one another
- Idle bears do small random hops with squash and stretch
- "Pour more bears" drops a handful from above into a wobbling, jiggling pile

UI
- Editorial product-page style on a white background. Large italic serif title "Gummy / Bears.", a short subtitle, a minimal card on the right with flavor swatches, a wobble slider, live "Stretch" and "Bounces" readouts and a "Pour more bears" button
- A subtle circular cursor that grows while grabbing
- ACES tone mapping, environment reflections, soft key and back light. Smooth 60fps

prompt.text:
Create a high-end cinematic and educational 3D animation in Three.js explaining how a Tesla-style electric motor works.

The animation must have an EXACT FIXED DURATION OF 40 SECONDS.

Do not make the animation shorter or longer than 40 seconds.

Final output:
Exact duration: 40.0 seconds
Resolution: 1920x1080
Aspect ratio: 16:9
Frame rate: 30 FPS
Total frames: 1200
High-quality anti-aliasing
High-resolution textures
Smooth deterministic animation
Extremely realistic visual quality

The overall visual quality should resemble a premium automotive engineering visualization or a high-end technical product commercial.

Build a detailed electric motor assembly inspired by the permanent-magnet AC motors used in modern Tesla vehicles. Do not use Tesla logos or branding.

FIXED TIMELINE

0–5 seconds — Hero introduction
Show the fully assembled electric motor suspended in a dark premium studio environment.

Use:
cinematic lighting
realistic brushed aluminum
copper
steel
magnets
insulation
bearings
realistic reflections
ambient occlusion
realistic shadows
subtle depth of field

Use a slow cinematic orbit around the motor.

During the final part of this section, make the outer housing partially transparent to reveal the internal structure.

5–11 seconds — Internal components
Move the camera closer and reveal the internal motor components.

Clearly show:
stator
copper windings
rotor
permanent magnets
motor shaft
bearings
housing
cooling channels
electrical connections

Highlight the important components one at a time.

Use floating labels with short technical names.

Keep non-highlighted components slightly darker or semi-transparent.

11–19 seconds — Exploded view
Create a dramatic and highly detailed exploded-view animation.

Separate the motor into many individual mechanical components along the motor axis.

Include:
outer housing
front cover
rear cover
bearings
shaft
rotor core
rotor magnets
stator core
copper windings
cooling components
seals
electrical connectors
fasteners

Keep every component perfectly aligned.

The viewer must clearly understand where every piece belongs.

Move the camera slightly through the exploded assembly while highlighting the major components.

Near the end of this section, smoothly begin reassembling the motor.

19–28 seconds — Electromagnetic operation
Finish reassembling the motor.

Explain how electricity creates rotation.

Visualize three-phase AC current flowing through the stator windings.

Use animated electrical pulses inside the copper coils.

Visualize the rotating magnetic field around the stator using elegant semi-transparent magnetic field lines, arrows, or vector effects.

Show how the rotating magnetic field interacts with the permanent magnets inside the rotor.

Clearly visualize magnetic attraction and repulsion.

The rotor should begin rotating slowly and gradually accelerate.

Display these short explanations:

"Three-phase current creates a rotating magnetic field."

"The magnetic field interacts with the rotor."

"This interaction generates torque."

28–34 seconds — Technical close-up and power flow
Show a close-up cross-section of the stator and rotor.

Visualize:
magnetic north and south poles
rotating stator magnetic field
rotor magnetic field
electric current direction
torque direction
rotor rotation direction

Optionally show three small animated sine waves representing phases A, B, and C, separated by 120 degrees.

Then visualize the complete energy conversion process:

Electrical energy
→ stator current
→ rotating magnetic field
→ electromagnetic torque
→ rotor rotation
→ mechanical output through the shaft.
Use clean animated arrows to show the energy flow.
34–38 seconds — High-speed operation
Show the motor operating at high RPM.
The rotor should spin smoothly while the stator remains stationary.
Add subtle motion blur.

Show cooling flow through the housing using translucent fluid paths.

Visualize heat being removed from the stator and copper windings.
38–40 seconds — Final hero shot

Transition back to the fully assembled motor.

Show a slow cinematic rotation.

Briefly use a transparent cutaway so the spinning rotor can still be seen inside.

Finish with the text:

"Electrical energy → Electromagnetic torque → Mechanical rotation"
The animation must end exactly at 40.0 seconds.

VISUAL QUALITY

The animation should be:

photorealistic

cinematic

technically believable

futuristic

premium
educational
clean and uncluttered
Avoid cartoon styling.
Use realistic:
machining details
bolts
screws

copper winding geometry

segmented magnets
bearing geometry
cooling channels
metallic surfaces
manufacturing details
Use physically based materials with:
metallic properties
roughness variation
normal maps
realistic reflections

subtle surface imperfections
CAMERA
Use only smooth cinematic camera movement:
slow orbit shots
macro close-ups
controlled dolly-ins

exploded-view fly-throughs

cross-section shots

internal motor views
Avoid:
shaky camera movement
sudden cuts
excessive zooming
unrealistic camera acceleration

ANIMATION REQUIREMENTS
All transitions must be smooth and deliberate.
The exploded-view sequence should be one of the main visual highlights.
All mechanical components must separate and reassemble with precise motion.
Electrical currents, magnetic fields, torque indicators, and rotor rotation must remain synchronized.

The entire animation must use the same fixed 40-second timeline on every execution so the prompt can be used as a repeatable benchmark between different AI coding and 3D generation systems.

title.zh: 巨型机器人动画场景模型对比
title.en: Giant Robot Anime Scene Model Comparison

summary.zh: 对比 Fable 5.5 与 Gemini 4 Argon。两者用同一段提示词，生成吉卜力风格的 2D 动画场景：长满青苔的巨型机器人在日出时起身，成品为单个 HTML 文件。
summary.en: A side-by-side comparison of Fable 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon. Each model made a Ghibli-style 2D anime scene of an overgrown giant robot rising at sunrise, delivered as a single HTML file from the same prompt.

prompt.text: Create a 2D anime scene for the web. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic. Deliver the final result as a single, self-contained HTML file. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything etc. Use Studio Ghibli films as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color, and atmosphere. Create an original giant robot as the main character. No people appear in the scene. Use any tools or techniques you want, including 3D, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime. SCENE At sunrise, mist hangs over an abandoned forest. A giant robot has knelt here for so long that moss, wildflowers, and old trees have grown over its body. A small bird lands on its shoulder as the first ray of sunlight reaches its weathered face. Deep inside its chest, a faint light flickers on. The ground trembles and birds burst from the treetops. With a deep, creaking groan, the robot slowly rises as soil, vines, and leaves pour from its armor. It lifts its head toward a gap in the canopy. The engines ignite, sending a great ring of wind across the forest. The robot tears into the golden sky, leaving a curving trail of light and mist as leaves spiral down through the sunbeams. ANIME QUALITY STANDARD Every frame must look as if it was drawn by professional anime animators and painted by master background artists for a finished theatrical film. Robot: A hand-drawn anime mecha that feels heavy, ancient, and full of personality, with cel-colored forms, chipped paint, rust, moss, and believable weathering. Keep it on-model from every angle, and let its posture and glowing eyes express emotion. Line art: Confident, delicate, hand-inked anime line work with subtle variation in thickness and pressure. Coloring: Traditional anime cel coloring with clean color areas, simple hard-edged shadows, and a soft, natural palette. Backgrounds: Richly detailed, hand-painted anime backgrounds in a gouache style, with visible brushwork, natural color variation, layered foliage, and real depth. Lighting: Golden sunrise light, colorful shadows, glowing mist, and soft atmosphere that unite the robot and background. Animation: Authentic hand-drawn anime timing with real weight, strong key poses, natural holds, and overlapping movement in vines, grass, leaves, birds, and falling debris. The robot should rise slowly and feel massive, then launch with explosive power. Direction: Cinematic anime shots, beautiful composition, thoughtful staging, and pacing that starts quietly, builds tension, and ends in a soaring climax. IT MUST NOT LOOK LIKE - 3D: No plastic materials, CGI shading, visible polygons, game-engine lighting, or computer-perfect perspective. - SVG or vector art: No simple geometric shapes, perfect curves, uniform outlines, flat corporate illustration, or basic gradients. - Web animation: No sliding layers, constant bobbing, floating parts, smooth software easing, or puppet-like joint rotation. You are free to change any part of the prompt, if it would result, in better results. - AI art: No warped shapes, melted details, flickering, or changing robot designs. - Non-anime art: No Western cartoon designs, realistic rendering, soft painterly shading on the robot, or generic digital illustration. - Amateur work: No stiff poses, empty backgrounds, repeated trees, muddy colors, clip art, placeholders, or unfinished details. The result should feel awe-inspiring, nostalgic, and full of wonder, like the moment an old forgotten dream comes back to life. Before finishing, inspect random frames as still images. If any frame does not look completely like real 2D anime, keep improving it. Do not stop until every frame could pass as a still from a theatrical anime film.

summary.en: The creator gave four models a detailed prompt for a mechanically accurate animated cutaway of a nine-cylinder radial aircraft engine.

prompt.text:
Build a 2D animated cutaway of a 9-cylinder radial aircraft engine called "RADIAL NINE" — a clean technical loop that shows how nine pistons share one crankshaft.
STYLE (strict)
Flat 2D technical front view on a deep navy background (#0b1220 or similar), like a premium engineering explainer.
Clean shapes with soft shading, thin light outlines, a subtle hatched pattern on cut metal walls.
Palette: light steel-grey metal; fresh fuel-air mixture in blue; combustion in orange to white; exhaust in smoky grey.
One square composition (1:1), the engine centred and filling ~80% of the square.
NO on-screen UI, no title, no labels by default. The only text is small cylinder numbers 1–9 engraved on the cylinder heads as part of the drawing.
THE ENGINE (must be mechanically correct)
Front view, with the propeller drawn as a faint translucent blur so the engine behind it stays visible.
Nine finned cylinders spaced evenly every 40° around a round crankcase, each cut open to show its piston.
Every cylinder head has an intake and an exhaust valve with rocker arms and pushrods.
A single-throw crankshaft in the centre. One master rod on cylinder 1 is attached directly to the crank pin; the other eight articulated link rods attach to pins on the master rod's big end, not to the crankshaft.
Because of the articulated rods, the pistons' motion is slightly non-uniform. Model the real linkage geometry rather than faking it with identical sine motion.
Four-stroke cycle: each cylinder fires once every two crankshaft revolutions.
Firing order 1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8, so the flashes jump around the ring skipping every other cylinder.
THE CYCLE (driven by one crank angle, all motion synchronized)
Intake: the intake valve opens and blue mixture flows in as the piston moves inward.
Compression: both valves closed, the mixture compresses and brightens.
Power: a spark and an orange flame front fill the cylinder and push the piston inward.
Exhaust: the exhaust valve opens and grey exhaust leaves through the exhaust stub.
Rockers and pushrods move in time with their valves.
Gases never pass through solid walls.
ANIMATION (starts on load)
Seamless loop of ~10–12 s at a readable speed (about one crankshaft revolution every 1.5 s), so the firing pattern reads as a spiral of flashes.
A brief 0.5× slow-down once per loop so the articulated rods can be followed.
Subtle heat glow on each cylinder head after it fires, slight engine vibration, the propeller blur spinning in sync with the crankshaft.
KEYBOARD (optional, nothing visible on screen)
Space pauses, S toggles slow motion, L toggles small labels (master rod, link rod, crank pin, intake, exhaust, spark plug), arrow keys change speed.
TECHNICAL
Canvas or SVG, any libraries you like (loaded from a CDN).
Everything works by opening index.html directly in the browser: no build step, no local server.
Starts automatically on load, no Start button. Smooth 60 fps.
The square stays centred and as large as possible at any window size, including phones.
Original content only.
When finished, open the page, check the firing order (1-3-5-7-9-2-4-6-8, each cylinder once per two revolutions), the articulated rod geometry, the loop and the browser console for errors, and fix any issues. Reply briefly with what was done and where the files are.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML page (no build step) showing an interactive 3D "Fluffy Watermelon" covered in long fur, rendered with WebGL using three.js r147 (UMD build: https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/three@0.147.0/build/three.min.js). All UI text in English.

SCENE & LOOK
- Full-screen canvas on a soft watermelon-flesh pink studio background: vertical gradient #ECB3AB → #F7CFC7 (lighter band in the middle) → #E8A9A0, used as the scene background.
- A big oblong watermelon lying on its side along the X axis: half-length 1.38, radius 0.98, blunt barrel-like ends, small dimples at both ends, slightly flattened belly, subtle surface unevenness. Start in a 3/4 view (about -0.32 rad around Y, 0.1 rad tilt), camera FOV 30°, framed to fill ~80% of the height.
- Rind pattern under the fur: light green (#A8D66B) with 16 dark green (#1C4D1C) stripes running stem to blossom, with ragged finger-like edges (sine meander + value noise), plus a pale cream "field spot" on the underside. Each hair takes the colour of its own root, so the stripes stay crisp through the fur.
- A short, dried, ribbed stem stub at one end with a slightly domed pale cut cap, and a thin curly helical tendril springing from beside it.
- One directional light from upper-left-front, wrap diffuse, Kajiya-Kay anisotropic highlight along the hair tangent, darker roots (occlusion by hair height), slight per-hair brightness variation.

FUR (most important: it must look crisp, never blurry)
- Fur length 0.2 units. Hairs grow out along the normal, then bend: combed from the stem end toward the blossom end and draped down the flanks (no whorls at the ends), plus slight gravity.
- Undercoat: shell texturing with ~64 instanced shells of the body mesh that reach only 50% of the fur length. Procedural hair cells in UV space (density scaled so one cell is ~3.4 device pixels at the default view), two hair populations (long + fine underfur), hairs gathering into locks toward their tips, analytic anti-aliased coverage, alpha blending, shells write depth. Fade shells out where the surface is seen edge-on and discard faint fragments, so no dotted rim appears at the outline.
- Guard hairs: ~90,000 individual tapered, camera-facing ribbon strands (instanced, 7 segments each) that follow exactly the same bend function, with a minimum width of ~0.75 px so they stay sharp. Draw them twice: once before the shells and once after (depth-tested), so faint edge fur never hides them and they always lie crisply on top.
- Always render at the device's full pixel ratio (capped at 2) and NEVER lower it for performance. If frames are slow, reduce the shell count first (down to 32), then the guard-hair count.

INTERACTION
- Drag to rotate freely (trackball style) with inertia after a flick. The fur lags behind the rotation through a damped spring and flops back. Gentle idle breeze in the fur; after 3 s without input, a slow auto-turn.
- Mouse wheel / pinch to zoom (smooth dolly). Double-click or "0" resets with an eased animation. Arrow keys rotate.
- Custom cursor: the native grab hand plus a thin dark 46 px ring that follows the pointer and shrinks while dragging. Hovering gently parts the fur under the cursor, as if stroking it.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion (no idle spin, no breeze).

UI & ROBUSTNESS
- Bottom-left caption: "Fluffy Watermelon" and a hint "Drag to rotate · Scroll to zoom · Double-click to reset" (on touch devices: "Drag to rotate · Pinch to zoom") that fades after the first interaction. Font: Onest from Google Fonts with system fallbacks.
- Guard against a zero-sized container at load: clamp width/height to at least 1 and, every frame, recover from any non-finite camera distance or rotation state.
- Show a small on-page note if the WebGL context is lost or a shader fails to compile, and a fallback message if WebGL is unavailable.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a simple 3D "Jelly Pumpkin" demo using three.js from a CDN. Keep the code short and basic.

SCENE
- One orange pumpkin in the centre made from a low-poly sphere (about 24x16 segments) with 8 shallow ribs, flat shading.
- MeshPhongMaterial, slightly transparent (opacity 0.9), bright orange with a little emissive colour. No transmission, no environment map, no post-processing.
- Jack-o'-lantern face made of flat black 2D shapes (two triangle eyes, triangle nose, zigzag mouth) placed just in front of the pumpkin surface. No glow from inside.
- Simple green cylinder stem on top.
- Three small low-poly pumpkins (purple, green, orange) and four small flattened spheres as candy around it.
- White background, ambient light plus one directional light, basic hard shadows on the floor.

INTERACTION
- Click the pumpkin: it squashes slightly (scale Y down, X/Z up) and springs back quickly with no extra wobble.
- Drag the stem: draw a straight thin green cylinder from the stem to the cursor. Dragging upward lifts the whole pumpkin rigidly; release and it falls, with one small bounce.
- "Carve Face" button: instantly swap to a second face (two black circle eyes, round mouth).
- "Glow" slider: changes the emissive intensity of the pumpkin a little.
- "Add Candy" button: drops 16 small spheres from above; they fall, bounce once on the floor and stop. No collision with the pumpkin.

UI
- Plain HTML: title "Jelly Pumpkin" in bold Arial top left, subtitle "Click the pumpkin to make it wobble!".
- Top right white box with border: colour buttons (Orange, Purple, Green), Glow range input, "Carve Face" and "Add Candy" buttons with default browser styling.
- Bottom left small grey text with stats: "Wobble: 0.6 | Face: 1 | Candy: 0".

summary.zh: 作品是一个循环播放的动画 SVG，描绘表情丰富的霸王龙努力骑自行车，并配有细致背景和喜剧化动作。
summary.en: The work is a looping animated SVG of an expressive T-rex struggling to ride a bicycle, with a detailed background and comic motion.

prompt.text:
Create an animated SVG: a T-rex trying to ride a bicycle. His tiny arms can't reach the handlebars.

THE CHARACTER
A big, expressive, original cartoon T-rex with a clear personality: a huge head, tiny arms, a thick tail, strong legs, big expressive eyes and eyebrows, a toothy grin that changes with what is happening (confident, worried, determined, embarrassed).

Good anatomy and proportions that read clearly even at a small size. Clean outlines, soft shading, a consistent art style.
THE BICYCLE
A real-looking bicycle with a frame, two wheels with spokes, a chain, pedals, a saddle, a bell and handlebars. It must look believable and mechanically correct: the chain moves, the pedals turn with the legs, the wheels spin at the right speed for the motion.
The T-rex's legs really pedal. The tiny arms keep reaching and failing to touch the handlebars.
THE COMEDY (the animation is about the struggle)
The T-rex tries to steer with his chin, his tail, his head, or by leaning, and the bike wobbles. He almost falls, recovers, then tries again.
Little gags that happen along the way: the bell rings by itself when he sneezes, his tiny arms flap in frustration, the tail swings and balances him, a small bird lands on his head or on the handlebars.
A funny moment of success (he steers perfectly for one second and looks proud) followed by a funny failure.
THE ANIMATION
Smooth, lively, cartoon-style motion with weight, squash and stretch, anticipation and follow-through. The body bobs with each pedal stroke, the tail lags behind, the bike bounces over small bumps.
The camera follows the T-rex, with the world moving past him in layers at different speeds for depth.
A seamless loop of about 12 seconds.
THE BACKGROUND
Make the background rich, detailed, atmospheric and full of life, with real depth and lots of small details to discover. It should feel like a full world, not an empty backdrop. Choose the setting and the mood yourself.
REQUIREMENTS
The animation is an SVG shown on a single web page (index.html) that opens directly in the browser, with no build step and no local server. You may use any animation approach you like (SVG animation, CSS, JavaScript).
It starts automatically and loops seamlessly. No buttons, no text, no interface.
One square (1:1) composition, centred and as large as possible at any window size, and it looks good on a phone.
Original characters and design only.

title.zh: 运河风车3D场景模型对比
title.en: 3D canal and windmill scene model comparison

summary.zh: 作者用一段详细的WebGPU/WGSL提示词让Opus 5.5制作出一个带物理水面、船只和野生动物的果冻风格运河船闸互动场景，效果优于用同一任务测试的ChatGPT-6 Astra和Gemini 4 Argon。
summary.en: Using a detailed WebGPU/WGSL prompt, Opus 5.5 built an interactive jelly diorama of an English canal lock scene with physics-based water, boats and wildlife, outperforming ChatGPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Argon on the same task.

prompt.text:
Build "Lock Jelly." — a single self-contained HTML file (WebGPU + WGSL, no libraries, no network, works from file://), part of a "Material Studies" series of jelly dioramas. If WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails, show a clean fallback card instead of the scene.

CONCEPT
A square block of clear coloured jelly (about 5.2 × 5.2 units, ~2 units high) holding a little English canal scene. The canal runs along the FRONT edge of the block, so the block's front face cuts the water lengthways: you see the lock chamber in cross-section, the water inside it rising and falling between the gates, fish swimming, the boat's hull below the waterline. All cut faces show candy-coloured soil strata; under the pounds a blue-grey puddle-clay lining, under the chamber a brick invert on a concrete bed, under the fields brown earth and turf.

LAYOUT (left to right along the front)
- Upper pound on the left at the higher level, opening into a round winding hole (a bay for turning boats); near the lock it narrows between brick wing walls.
- The lock chamber in the middle: brick walls with dressed-stone quoins and coping, a slimy band between the two water levels and weed below, an iron ladder, a gauge board, a stone cill under the top gate, recesses that the open gates fold into.
- Below the bottom gate a short walled tail, then the lower pound bends away from the front face, runs under a humpback brick bridge into a basin with a willow-covered island, lily pads in its corners and a sunken bicycle on the bed.
- The ground steps down from an upper terrace to a lower one along a grassy bank.
- Behind the lock: stone setts around the chamber, bollards, a gravel towpath, a lane, the keeper's whitewashed cottage with a slate roof, green door, picket-fence garden full of flowers and washing flapping on a line, a gas lamp, a bench, a white windmill with turning lattice sails, oaks, willows, poplars, a hedge, sheep, reeds on the soft banks.

WATER
- Linear shallow-water waves on a staggered grid (~168²) with a little surface tension, so short ripples are springy like jelly; damping and firmness are adjustable.
- Three separate bodies of water — upper pound, chamber, lower pound — each with its own rest level. Faces between bodies stay shut unless the gate between them is open and the levels are equal. The chamber's level is moved bodily when paddles are drawn (Torricelli-style flow), with boils, white water and a dimple at the intake.
- Rendering: refraction of the scene behind, flavour-coloured absorption, sun caustics on the bed, soft light shafts, foam (wakes, paddle churn), a meniscus line on the cut faces. Split the surface mesh along the gate lines so the step in level at a shut gate is a clean wall hidden by the gate leaf, not a ramp.
- The block itself can be tipped by dragging its side; the jelly shears and wobbles, the water sloshes, and it settles back.

THE LOCK AND THE KEEPER
- Two single-leaf timber gates (planks, rails, diagonal brace, iron straps, a walkway with a handrail), each with a white balance beam with black bands. Ground-paddle pedestals with toothed racks that rise when wound.
- An articulated lock keeper (flat cap, navy jumper, cords, windlass in hand; torso, arms, thighs and shins as separate parts). He walks with a proper gait, plans his route around the bench, pedestals, bollards and any beam lying across his way (going round the beam's end), leans his back on a beam and walks it round backwards to swing a gate, winds the windlass with his arm circling the spindle, and sits on his bench between jobs. He sets off for the gate as the boat comes in.
- The cycle: the boat lies in the full chamber → keeper shuts the top gate → winds up the bottom paddles → the chamber empties into the tail with white water → winds them down → opens the bottom gate → the boat leaves, runs the tail, swings round the bend, ducks under the bridge, goes round the island and comes back into the chamber bow first → shut bottom gate → round to the top paddles → chamber fills with boils → open the top gate → the boat goes up the pound, turns in the winding hole and comes back. Repeat forever. A gate may only open when the levels match.

BOATS
- A traditional narrowboat "Wobble": black lofted hull, a green cabin with red lining-out, brass portholes, a cratch board and cover at the bow, a chimney with brass bands (puffing smoke), a painted Buckby can, plank and pole on the roof, rope fenders, a headlamp, a brass swan-neck tiller and a steerer in a red jumper. It follows smooth filleted routes (check the stern never swings out through the block's face), slows near the gates, heaves, pitches and rolls on the local surface, and hands its displaced volume back to the water so it makes bow waves and wakes.
- Three moored narrowboats in the basin in different liveries with flowerpots on the roofs and one ginger cat, tied to bank pins with stretchy mooring lines.

LIFE
- Roach, perch and bream as boids that stay in their own body of water (they can only move between pound and chamber while a gate is open), under the surface and hulls, off the bed, scattering from the boat and splashes.
- Mallards (drakes, ducks) and a duck with four ducklings that follow exactly along her trail; a pair of mute swans in the basin. They paddle the surface, ride the chamber down and up, upend now and then, get out of the boat's way and come for bread.
- A grey heron that wades in the shallows or stands on a moored boat's roof, stabs at fish (sometimes catching one), and flaps off somewhere quieter when the boat passes or someone toots.
- Chimney smoke from the boat and the cottage.

UI (editorial, like a print magazine)
- Top-left: small caps eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a huge italic serif title "Lock / Jelly.", a short subtitle. Top-right: a status pill "WebGPU · Live / Paused / Unavailable".
- Right: a frosted-glass control panel (a bottom sheet on mobile) with: buttons Hurry (speeds the keeper, paddles and boat), Toot (horn; also Space), Throw bread, Rubber duck (drops a yellow rubber duck that floats upright, can be picked up and thrown, rides the lock, is stopped by gates and shoved by boats); a liveliness meter; tallies Trips · Lockfuls · Fed; a status line "Wobble — Emptying the lock 62%" telling the story step by step; three flavours Greengage, Elderflower, Blackcurrant (change the water colour/absorption and strata); sliders Firmness, Wave damping, Paddle speed; Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, View.
- Bottom-left: "How to play — Throw bread. Toot the horn. Hurry the keeper." with a small line of instructions.
- Interaction: drag across the water to make waves, drag the block's side to tip it, pick up and throw rubber ducks, drag empty space to orbit, scroll/pinch to zoom; touch works.
- Soft studio lighting on a warm paper backdrop with the block's tinted, caustic-flecked shadow; WebAudio sounds: the boat's horn, the gate thudding shut, a creak, the windlass ratchet, and the rush of water that swells with the flow.

QUALITY
Keep it smooth (fixed-step physics, cheap per frame), no console errors, no page scroll, works at phone width. Test it headlessly: a full round trip happens, levels go exactly from upper to lower and back, no gate opens across a step, the keeper never walks into the water or through obstacles, the boat never touches a gate leaf, and every button works.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: an interactive 3D toy called "Jelly Bricks" - translucent gummy candy bricks you can grab, stretch, stack into a tower and knock over. Use three.js (import from a CDN) and any lightweight physics library you like. Everything must run by opening the file in a browser.

LOOK
- Bricks are classic stud-on-top building bricks (2x1, 2x2, 3x2, 4x2) in red, orange, yellow, green and blue. No brand names or logos anywhere.
- Material must read as real gummy candy: glossy, translucent, light passing through, deeper colour where the brick is thicker, soft rounded edges and rounded studs. Use MeshPhysicalMaterial with transmission, thickness, attenuation colour, clearcoat, and an environment map for reflections.
- Soft shadows plus a faint coloured glow on the floor under each brick, tinted by its colour.
- Clean white background, slight slow camera drift so the scene feels alive.

JELLY BEHAVIOUR (most important)
- Grab a brick and it stretches toward the cursor before it lifts off, like pulling taffy. Release it and the stretch snaps back with a decaying wobble.
- A brick lagging behind the cursor tilts slightly in the direction it's moving.
- Every landing squashes the brick flat, then it springs back up with a few wobbles (spring-damper squash and shear, done in the vertex shader).
- Dropping a brick on the stack snaps it in place, and the whole tower sways like pudding: each brick's wobble shifts the bricks above it, so the top moves the most.
- Pulling a brick out of the middle of the tower collapses it: the bricks above tumble, bounce off the floor and each other, and scatter a little - lively, not explosive.

UI (minimal editorial style)
- Top left: small caps label "Nº 09 / SOFT GOODS", big serif italic title "Jelly / Bricks." with "Bricks." in red, and a one-line subtitle.
- Floating panel on the right: flavor colour swatches, a "Wobble" slider that controls jelly softness, live "Stack height" and "Bricks" counters, and a black "Pour more bricks" button that drops a handful of new bricks from above with random spin.
- Bottom left hint: "Grab to lift · Drop to snap · Space to wobble". Space shakes the tower.
- Custom round cursor that shrinks while holding a brick.

Start with one 4x2 brick in the centre as the tower base and about 9 bricks scattered around it. Keep it at 60fps on a laptop.

title.zh: 港口果冻交互立体模型对比

summary.zh: 一个名为“Harbor Jelly”的互动WebGPU 3D场景，展示果冻质感海水中的集装箱港口，由Claude Opus 5.5根据一段详细的长提示词生成，并与Gemini 4 Argon版本比较了制作成本。
summary.en: An interactive WebGPU 3D diorama called 'Harbor Jelly' depicting a container port inside a jelly-like sea, built with Claude Opus 5.5 from a long detailed prompt, and compared in cost to a Gemini 4 Argon version of the same scene.

prompt.text: Build "Harbor Jelly" — a single self-contained HTML file (no external requests, no libraries) that renders an interactive 3D diorama with WebGPU/WGSL: a small working container harbor set inside a square block of wobbly, translucent jelly sea, sitting on a paper studio backdrop. It belongs to a series called "Material Studies", so match that look: warm paper background, serif italic display title ("Harbor Jelly."), small uppercase eyebrow "MATERIAL STUDIES", a status pill top-right ("WebGPU · Live"), a frosted control panel on the right, and a "How to play" line bottom-left. English UI. Light theme only, by design. THE BLOCK - A 5.2 × 5.2 block seen from a 3/4 orbit camera. The ground and sea are cut flat at the block's sides, so you see candy-coloured soil strata in cross-section, and the sea's cut faces show everything underwater through the jelly. - The water is a real-time linear shallow-water simulation on a staggered grid (heights at cell centres, velocities on faces) with a little surface tension, so it feels like jelly. Render it with refraction, absorption by depth, caustics projected onto the floor, light shafts, a Fresnel studio reflection, foam (wakes, splashes, a shoreline lace) and a bright meniscus on the cut edges. - The whole block can be tipped by dragging its side. The water sloshes to the low side, the jelly shears and quivers, then it settles flat again. THE HARBOR (layout) - Along the back runs a vertical concrete quay wall, with rubber fenders, bollards, ladders, and mussels and weed crusting it below the waterline. - Left part: a container terminal. A flat asphalt yard with painted lines, concrete strips with two crane rails, light towers, and a small terminal office. Hundreds of colourful containers are stacked in neat rows. Each is a ribbed steel box with door ends and darker corner posts, drawn as GPU instances in about ten liveries. - Right part: an old stone fishing quay with a cobbled promenade, a corrugated fish-market shed and lamp posts. A timber pier stands on mussel-covered piles with cross-bracing, with two small fishing boats moored alongside. - Behind it all, a town climbs a grassy hill: three rows of gabled houses in Nordic harbour colours (falu red, ochre, white, pale blue, mint, pink) with tiled or slate roofs, white-framed windows, doors and chimneys. There is a white church with a green copper spire, and some round trees. - A rubble breakwater shelters the fishing harbour, with a concrete crown wall. Big rocks sit near the crest, smaller weedy ones tumble down under water. On its head stands a red-and-white banded lighthouse with a gallery and a glass lantern, whose lamp slowly turns. - In the open basin: two small yachts swinging on their moorings (white hulls, coloured stripe, fin keels visible through the jelly, furled sails), yellow mooring buoys, and a green channel buoy, all bobbing on the waves. - On the floor: pale sand with drifts of silt, weed tufts, stones, starfish, an old anchor with chain, a lost tyre. THE SHIP'S DAY (fully automatic loop, about 100 s) 1. A small feeder container ship (navy topsides, red antifouling, white accommodation block at the stern with bridge wings, funnel with a yellow band, turning radar, visible propeller) lies alongside with containers on deck, 6 bays × 4 rows × 2 tiers. 2. Two ship-to-shore gantry cranes on the rails, one red and one blue, each with portal legs, a backreach with a machinery house, an A-frame with forestays, a hinged boom, a trolley with a hanging cab, and a yellow spreader on four wire falls. They lower their booms and swap boxes: unload from the tops of the ship's stacks into yard stacks, then load other boxes aboard. Every move is a smooth sequence: travel, trolley out, lower onto the box (tracking the ship's bobbing), latch, hoist, trolley across, lower, unlatch. Cranes never get closer than their leg width; an idle crane moves out of the other's way. 3. When the work is done the trolleys park, the booms swing up, and a tug comes round to the bow. The tug has a black hull, white and red superstructure, a tyre fender all round, a big bow fender, and puffs of funnel smoke. It passes a tow line and backs away, pulling the bow off the quay while the ship swings out. Then the line is cast off, the tug pivots on the spot and goes home, and the ship sounds her horn. 4. The ship sails a lap of the harbour along a smooth path, past the lighthouse. She rides the water on several sample points (heave, pitch, roll) and hands the displaced water back to the sim, so she leaves a real bow wave, wake and white water. 5. Meanwhile the tug goes out to a standby spot. When the ship stops off the quay, the tug noses in and pushes her sideways onto the fenders, with prop wash churning. Then it backs off, the booms come down, and the cranes start again. - Keep everything collision-free (ship and tug vs. quay, breakwater, pier, yachts and buoy; no grounding). Check it with a headless node test. LIFE - Fish schools (mackerel, herring, small orange wrasse) as boids that stay in the water and under the hulls, scatter from fingers, splashes and moving ships, and come to food. - Moon jellyfish: glassy pulsing bells with four pink rings, frilly oral arms and a fringe of tentacles. They drift with the water flow. - Herring gulls (white body, grey mantle, black wingtips, yellow bill with a red spot). They circle, bank and glide, and land on perches: lamps, roof ridges, the church spire, the lighthouse gallery, the crane apexes, the ship's mast, the tug, the yachts' masthead. Perches on moving things move with them. They all take off when the horn sounds, and some dive at food. - Steam puffs from the ship's funnel on the horn; tiny bubbles caught in the jelly. CONTROLS (right panel; bottom sheet on phones) - "Cast off" sends the ship early (cranes finish the box in hand). At sea the button becomes "Call her in" and hurries her home; it greys out while busy. - "Horn" (also Space) plays a synthesized WebAudio ship horn: two low detuned sawtooth reeds a fifth apart, low-passed, starting only after a user gesture. It also blows steam and scatters the gulls. - "Feed the fish" scatters pellets off the end of the pier; fish rush in and gulls swoop down. - Tally: Boxes moved / Voyages / Fed. A ship status line ("Unloading 3 / 8", "Loading", "Booms up", "Tug coming", "Casting off", "At sea 40%", "Coming in", "Berthing"). A small activity meter. - Flavour swatches change the water colour and strata: Sea glass (teal-mint), Blueberry (deep blue), Lime. - Sliders: Firmness, Wave damping, Tide (±10 cm; the sea level, ships and floating things follow). - Buttons: Reset, Pause, Sound on/off, Reset view. POINTER INTERACTION - Drag across the water to make waves (with a crosshair cursor). - Drag the side of the block to tip it. - Pick up an orange-and-white lifebuoy and throw it. Lifebuoys float flat on the waves, bounce off the pier, buildings and breakwater, and are shoved aside by the ship and tug. - Drag empty space or right-drag to orbit; scroll or pinch to zoom. - On phones: touch orbit, pinch zoom, and a collapsible bottom sheet for the controls. RENDERING DETAILS - Pipeline: shadow map → caustics pass → opaque scene (with a distance buffer) → back-face pass of the water → water pass over a copy of the scene → tone map + dither. - Moving rigs are static vertex buffers whose vertices carry an object id; about 24 object transforms (position + quaternion) live in the uniform buffer. Cables are drawn with one end in each object's frame, so they stretch: crane falls, forestays, the tow line. - Material kinds in the prop shader: matte paint, glass, gloss steel, roof tiles, timber grain, corrugated sheet (normal-perturbed ribs), dressed-stone masonry, rubber, rock, glowing lamps, swaying weed, and hulls with antifouling below a boot-top line. - The jelly shear and squash wobble applies to everything inside the block. QUALITY BAR - Smooth on a laptop; simulation under about 2 ms per frame. - A friendly fallback screen if WebGPU is missing or the adapter fails. - No console errors, no page scroll. Respect prefers-reduced-motion. - Ship it with a headless test of the choreography and a Playwright end-to-end test.

- Concrete platform with a yellow tactile strip, a shelter with a corrugated roof, benches, a hanging clock, a small station building with a teal gable roof and a "春風駅" sign, a station name board (はるかぜ / Harukaze, with neighbouring stations), vending machines, bins, lamps, fence.

summary.en: The creator gave the same detailed prompt to Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-6 Astra to build a Three.js browser scene of a marine lagoon with sharks, whales and rays, comparing visuals and API cost across models.

prompt.text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file (inline CSS and JS; the only external script is Three.js r128 from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/three.js/r128/three.min.js) called "Reef Lagoon": an interactive top-down view of a sunlit Maldives-style lagoon where the user throws sea creatures into the water and watches them swim. Output the complete file, no placeholders, no omitted sections.

CAMERA AND LAYOUT
- Perspective camera straight overhead (height ~26 world units, up vector (0,0,-1)). Fit the vertical FOV so the visible water is about ±8.4 units in the short screen direction; the long direction scales with the aspect ratio. Recompute on resize.
- The whole screen is water. One world unit is roughly 1 m at toy scale: dolphin ~2.4, white shark ~3.3, hammerhead ~3.1, orca ~4.5, humpback ~6, turtle ~1.35 shell length, manta ~1.6 length / 3.2 wingspan.

WATER SIMULATION
- GPU ripple height field (ping-pong float/half-float render targets, about 440 texels on the long side, stepped at 90 Hz). Update: average of 4 neighbours, velocity += (avg − h)*1.8, velocity *= 0.9935, h += velocity, h *= 0.9993. Absorbing "sponge" edges, so waves leaving the screen don't reflect.
- Drops are queued (x, z, radius, amplitude, foam) and applied with a smooth cosine bump; a second channel stores foam that diffuses and fades.

RENDERING (draw order per frame)
1. A tileable animated caustics texture (512², mipmapped).
2. A shadow pass: creature geometry projected along the sun onto the floor, rendered from the main camera into a half-res target with MAX blending.
3. The underwater scene into an off-screen target. Its alpha stores depth*0.22, which later scales refraction and blur.
- Floor: a large heightfield mesh. Depth goes from ~1.35 near the bottom of the screen to ~4.3 at the top, with gentle undulation.
- Coral heads come from noise masks: raised 1–1.4 units, warm ochre/purple/yellow colours with knobbly and brain-coral detail, plus a rubble ring around them.
- Pale sand with soft irregular ripple shading.
- Lighting: ambient + sun × (base + caustics focused by the Laplacian of the ripple field) × shadow × drifting cloud shadows (large slow noise).
- Water absorption along the light path plus the view path, e.g. T = exp(−(0.30, 0.058, 0.04)·path), plus depth-based turquoise→blue scatter.
4. A full-screen water-surface pass. Each pixel is ray-cast through the inverse view-projection to the plane y=0.
- Surface normal from the ripple field + scrolling wind-ripple gradient noise + a gentle swell.
- Refraction: offset sampling of the underwater target, with chromatic split and depth blur.
- Fresnel sky reflection with clouds, sun glints, foam, splash craters (a short-lived analytic bowl around each impact; brighten it, never let it go dark), and an optional whirlpool funnel with spiral foam arms.
- Mild tone curve.
5. An overlay pass, depth-tested, drawn after the surface: creatures above water, water droplets (point sprites, gravity 20), soft mist sprites, rain streaks, expanding ring quads, and a drop-target marker.

CREATURES (procedural geometry, no external models)
- Local frame: nose at +x (x=0.5), tail toward −x, up +y, body length 1.
- Body: lofted elliptical cross-sections along x. Half-width W(u), half-height H(u) and centre offset C(u) are Catmull-Rom curves through control points, where u runs 0 at the nose to 1 at the tail. Flatten the belly, cap the ends, compute normals from the grid.
- Fins: thin double-sided sheets made as bilinear patches between a root chord and a tip chord, with bowed leading and trailing edges.
- Species:
1. Great white shark: slate-grey back with a ragged countershading line to a white belly, gill slits, tall triangular dorsal fin, big swept pectorals with dark tips underneath, crescent tail with a longer upper lobe.
2. Great hammerhead: flat wide cephalofoil with eyes at its tips, bronze-grey colour, tall sickle dorsal fin.
3. Humpback whale: near-black back, mottled white belly with throat pleats, knobs on the head, very long scalloped white pectorals, small dorsal hump, serrated flukes.
4. Orca: black, with the white eye patch, white chin, belly and flank lobe, grey saddle behind a towering dorsal fin, paddle-shaped pectorals.
5. Bottlenose dolphin: beak and melon forehead, dark cape over grey flanks and a pale belly, curved dorsal fin.
6. Green sea turtle: domed shell with scute pattern and amber streaks, pale belly plate, scaly head, long front flippers and small rear flippers.
7. Manta ray: diamond-shaped swept-back wings, curled horn-like fins at the mouth, whip tail, black top with white shoulder chevrons, white spotted belly.
- Draw each species as one InstancedBufferGeometry. Per-instance data: position, orientation quaternion, (swim phase, wave amplitude, turn, fin phase), (scale, alpha, body arch, fin amplitude), (seed, water-class flag, wetness, flipper angle offset).
- Vertex shader:
- Swimming body wave: side to side for sharks, up and down for whales, orca and dolphins, none for turtle and manta.
- Amplitude envelope grows toward the tail, plus turn curvature and arch.
- Rotate each cross-section to stay perpendicular to the bent spine.
- Rotate flippers on hinges about the body axis.
- Manta wing beat travels outward with amplitude ∝ |z|^1.45.
- Sample the GPU water height at the vertex for the waterline.
- Render each species in three passes: under water (discard fragments above the local water height, tint by water), above water (discard below), shadow (project to the floor). Also render card thumbnails with the same materials.
- Fade with an ordered (Bayer) dither. Lighting: sky/ground ambient, sun diffuse with caustics under water, glossy specular that increases when wet, rim light, eyes as dark spheres in the shader.

BEHAVIOUR
- Swimming: wander steering inside the screen (stay above the bottom dock UI), separation between creatures, preferred depth with floor clearance, pitch toward the target depth, roll into turns, currents from the whirlpool.
- Whales, orcas and dolphins periodically surface to breathe and spout: droplet column plus soft mist sprites plus a blow sound. Humpback spout is bushy, orca tall, dolphin a small puff. The humpback dives fluke-up.
- Sharks often cruise with the dorsal fin cutting the surface and leaving a V-wake of small drops.
- Turtles surface to breathe; mantas glide with wing beats.
- Dolphins porpoise-leap often; orca, humpback, shark and manta occasionally breach. A breach means rising fast, launching out of the water with an exit splash, then re-entering in the species style below.
- Tapping the water makes ripples. Sharks, dolphins and orcas come to look at the spot; turtles and mantas flee.

ENTERING THE WATER: EACH SPECIES DIFFERENT (the core feature)
- Tapping a creature card throws the creature from the card's screen position (projected onto the water plane, y=0.6) along a ballistic arc to a random free spot.
- Per-species gravity (whale 6.2, orca 7.5, dolphin 11, others 10) and flight time (whale 1.8 s, orca 1.5, hammerhead 1.3, manta 1.35, shark 1.2, dolphin 1.15, turtle 1.0). Start velocity: vy = (−y0 + ½gT²)/T.
- In the air, orientation is scripted against flight progress τ ∈ [0,1], relative to the trajectory pitch, and blended in from the start orientation over the first 22%:
- Shark: noses steeply down for a knife entry; tail thrashes.
- Hammerhead: corkscrews, two full rolls.
- Humpback: rolls onto its back (≈2.75 rad) and levels out, pectorals raised, body arched: a backflop.
- Orca: rolls onto its side (≈1.5 rad) and levels out.
- Dolphin: follows the arc for a clean head-first dive.
- Turtle: wobbles with flippers flapping into a belly-flop.
- Manta: forward somersault (−2π) into a flat wing slap, wings beating.
- Each entry has its own splash: a crater drop plus several drops along the body line for long animals, expanding rings, a droplet crown with species-specific counts and speeds, mist, bubbles, and sound.
- Dolphin: tiny "rip" splash.
- Sharks: tall crown; hammerhead adds spiral droplets.
- Humpback: huge white curtain (~500 droplets), mist and a low boom.
- Orca: big side splash.
- Turtle: low flat plop.
- Manta: wide low sheet of spray and a sharp slap.
- After entry the creature decelerates under water with a bubble trail, slerps back to its swimming orientation over 1.6–3.2 s (the whale rolls back over from its back), then swims.
- Dragging a card holds the creature above the water under the pointer (with a target ring on the water) and drops it on release with its own entry style.
- The user can grab any creature from the water (pick by distance to its projected body axis), carry it, and throw it back.

UI (English)
- Frosted-glass dock at the bottom: 7 creature cards with thumbnails rendered from the real models and a short description each ("Knifes straight in", "Corkscrew dive", "Backflop breach", "Lands on its side", "Clean arc dive", "Belly plop", "Wing slap"). On phones show short names.
- Tool buttons: Rain (streaks, ring ripples, dimmer sun), Whirlpool (draggable vortex that carries creatures), Calm, Clear (all creatures swim off and fade), Sound (synthesized Web Audio: splashes, plops, blows, slaps, booms, occasional humpback song, dolphin whistles, orca calls, ambient water), Hide UI.
- Top-left name plate "Reef Lagoon" with a live creature count; toasts and a hint line.
- Keyboard: 1–7 throw creatures, R W C M H.

QUALITY AND ROBUSTNESS
- Works on desktop and mobile (touch, pointer events, no horizontal overflow) and in both WebGL2 and WebGL1.
- Adaptive pixel ratio when frames are slow.
- Caps: 24 creatures total, max 3 humpbacks.
- Start with two dolphins, a turtle, a shark and a manta already swimming; a humpback breaches 1 s after load.
- Show a toast for runtime errors and lost WebGL contexts.
